passages.t: ‘Taste and see that the LORD is good’
passages.happening:
The heading gives a setting: “Of David, when he pretended to be insane before Abimelech, so that the king drove him away” (verse 1). Then the song: “I will bless the LORD at all times; His praise will always be on my lips” (verse 1).

He invites others in. “Magnify the LORD with me; let us exalt His name together” (verse 3). And he tells what happened: “I sought the LORD, and He answered me; He delivered me from all my fears” (verse 4). “This poor man called out, and the LORD heard him; He saved him from all his troubles” (verse 6).

“The angel of the LORD encamps around those who fear Him, and he delivers them” (verse 7). Then the famous invitation: “Taste and see that the LORD is good; blessed is the man who takes refuge in Him!” (verse 8).

“Young lions go lacking and hungry, but those who seek the LORD lack no good thing” (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
The heading points to a strange, humiliating moment in David's life. Running from Saul, he fled to the Philistine city of Gath. When the king's servants recognised him, he was afraid, so “he changed his behavior before them and feigned madness”, scratching on the gate and dribbling into his beard (1 Samuel 21:13). The king sent him away.

1 Samuel calls that king Achish, not Abimelech. Some think Abimelech was a title for Philistine kings, as Pharaoh was for Egypt's (a king of Gerar is called Abimelech in Genesis 20 and 26). Others think the heading is a later note that slipped in the name. The psalm itself does not mention the story.

Like Psalm 25, this is an alphabet poem: each verse begins with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet, with one letter missing and an extra last verse. It is a song of thanks that turns into teaching.

‘The angel of the LORD’ is God's messenger, who in some Old Testament stories speaks as God himself (Exodus 3:2-6). Here he ‘encamps around’ the faithful, like an army camped round a city to guard it.
passages.later:
Peter writes to Christians “now that you have tasted that the Lord is good” (1 Peter 2:3), using verse 8.

Hebrews says the angels are “ministering spirits sent to serve those who will inherit salvation” (Hebrews 1:14). When Elisha's servant was terrified of an army, God opened his eyes and “he saw that the hills were full of horses and chariots of fire all around Elisha” (2 Kings 6:17): verse 7 made visible.
passages.hard:
‘Those who seek the LORD lack no good thing’ (verse 10). But believers do sometimes go hungry, lose jobs and fall ill. Is the psalm wrong?

The psalm speaks as a thankful man telling what God did for him, and as a teacher pointing to how God's world usually goes. It is not a contract that promises every believer comfort. The next part of the psalm says, “Many are the afflictions of the righteous” (verse 19). Psalm 37 raises the same question, and Psalm 73 wrestles with it honestly. ‘No good thing’ means no good God sees we need, and above all God himself.
passages.asks:
Notice where David was when he learned this: not in a palace but pretending to be mad in an enemy city. Thanks can come from humiliating places.

‘Taste and see’ is an invitation, not an argument. You cannot know a food by reading about it. The psalm asks you to try trusting God, and find out.

passages.t: ‘Seek peace and pursue it’, and ‘not one of them will be broken’
passages.happening:
Now he teaches like a father. “Come, children, listen to me; I will teach you the fear of the LORD” (verse 11).

“Who is the man who delights in life, who desires to see good days? Keep your tongue from evil and your lips from deceitful speech. Turn away from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it” (verses 12-14).

God sees both kinds of people. “The eyes of the LORD are on the righteous, and His ears are inclined to their cry” (verse 15), but “the face of the LORD is against those who do evil” (verse 16).

Then two lines many have held on to in grief. “The LORD is near to the brokenhearted; He saves the contrite in spirit” (verse 18). “Many are the afflictions of the righteous, but the LORD delivers him from them all” (verse 19). “He protects all his bones; not one of them will be broken” (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
‘Come, children, listen to me’ is how the teachers of Proverbs speak to their students. ‘The fear of the LORD’ is not terror. It is the deep respect that shapes a whole life.

Notice what a good life looks like here. Most of it is speech (verse 13) and peace (verse 14). Peace is not waited for. It is chased: ‘seek peace and pursue it.’

‘Contrite’ in verse 18 means crushed, broken down. The psalm does not say God is near only to the strong. He is near to those who are falling apart.

Verse 20 is a picture of complete protection. In that world, broken bones from a beating or a fall could mean a life of pain, or death. The psalm says God keeps the righteous whole.
passages.later:
Peter quotes verses 12 to 16 to Christians who were being mistreated, and tells them not to repay evil for evil: “Whoever would love life and see good days must keep his tongue from evil and his lips from deceitful speech. He must turn from evil and do good; he must seek peace and pursue it” (1 Peter 3:10-11).

Jesus said, “Blessed are the peacemakers” (Matthew 5:9), and “Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted” (Matthew 5:4).

When Jesus died, the soldiers did not break his legs, as they did those of the men crucified with him. John writes, “Now these things happened so that the Scripture would be fulfilled: ‘Not one of His bones will be broken.’” (John 19:36). John does not say which Scripture he means. It may be verse 20 of this psalm, about the righteous man. It may be the law of the Passover lamb, whose bones were not to be broken (Exodus 12:46; Numbers 9:12). Many readers think John has both in mind: Jesus as the righteous sufferer and as the Passover lamb.
passages.hard:
‘The LORD delivers him from them all’ (verse 19). Yet many faithful people have died young, been imprisoned or been killed. Jesus himself was not spared the cross.

The psalm says two things together: the righteous have ‘many afflictions’, and God delivers them. It does not say the afflictions will be few or short. Christians read the final deliverance as resurrection. Jesus' bones were not broken, but he still died; and God brought him through death, not around it.

If you are brokenhearted now, verse 18 is not a sentence to argue with. It is one to rest on: God is near.
passages.asks:
Verses 13 and 14 are practical. What would ‘pursuing peace’ look like this week, with one particular person?

And if you feel crushed, read verse 18 again. The psalm does not ask you to be strong first. God comes near to the broken.
